food.text: Aboriginal Australians ate native animal and plant foods for an estimated 60,000 years of human habitation. An estimated 4,999 species of native food were used. Since much of it was unsafe or unpalatable raw, it was cooked on open fires, boiled in bark containers, pounded, or soaked by hanging bags in running water.

Bush tucker includes animal foods such as kangaroo, emu and witchetty grubs. Plant foods include fruits such as quandong, spices such as lemon myrtle, and vegetables such as warrigal greens and various native yams. Aboriginal Australians drew on these foods long before European settlement.

The First Fleet reached Sydney Harbour in 1788, and the settlers' diet consisted of bread, salted meat and tea with lashings of rum. The rum was initially from the West Indies. Meat made up a large share of the colonial diet.
The British found familiar game in Australia, including swan, goose, pigeon and fish. Even so, the new settlers often had difficulty adjusting to the prospect of native fauna as a staple diet.

During the colonial period, beef cattle, sheep and wheat became staples of the local diet. Culinary tastes were strongly influenced by British and Irish migrants after 1788. Meat made up a large proportion of what Australians ate.
Aboriginal Tasmanians were primarily nomadic. They moved with the seasons according to changing food supplies such as seafood, land mammals, native vegetables and berries.

A common Aboriginal cooking technique was to throw a carcass directly onto a campfire to roast it. After the First Fleet arrived in Botany Bay in 1788, native food sources were used to supplement the colonists' diet.

When the Māori of Poverty Bay met James Cook's HMS Endeavour in 1769, they quickly adopted the Europeans' metal cookware. The Māori had cooked without pottery, relying on earth ovens and stone boiling.

By the mid-18th century in northern Australia, trade and cross-cultural engagement had been established between local Aboriginal groups and Makassan trepangers. The trepangers visited from present-day Indonesia.

Colonisation beginning in 1788 severely affected the traditional use of bush foods. The introduction of non-native organisms and the destruction of traditional lands and habitats reduced Aboriginal people's access to native foods.

After harvest, Māori stored kūmara in rua kūmara, subterranean pits sealed with small wooden doors to keep out pests. These became common across Aotearoa after 1500 AD, and control over them was an important social distinction in classical Maori society.

In the pits, kūmara were placed on shelves cut into the walls and regularly checked for rot and rotated to stay dry. In the Bay of Plenty, the pits were often used for single seasons and backfilled afterwards, because of the soft tephra soil.

art.text: Aboriginal Australian art is described as the oldest unbroken tradition of art in the world. Evidence of it in Australia dates back at least 30,000 years, long before any European artist arrived.

The first artistic representations of Australia by European artists were mostly natural history illustrations. They showed the distinctive plants and animals of the land for scientific purposes, along with the topography of the coast.

Sydney Parkinson was the botanical illustrator on James Cook's 1770 voyage, which first charted the eastern coastline of Australia. Working under the direction of naturalist Joseph Banks, he made a large number of drawings.

George Stubbs painted Portrait of a Large Dog and The Kongouro from New Holland in 1772, showing a dingo and a kangaroo. In the form of copies and reproductions, they were the first images of Australian fauna to be widely disseminated in Britain.

Early Western art in Australia, from British colonisation in 1788 onwards, is often told as a gradual shift from a European sense of light to an Australian one. The lighting in Australia is notably different from Europe's, and early landscapes tried to reflect this.

Indigenous Australian art covers a very wide range of media, including painting on leaves, bark painting, wood carving, rock carving, sculpting, ceremonial clothing and sandpainting. Traditional visual symbols vary widely between peoples, despite the mistaken perception that dot painting represents all Aboriginal art.
Aboriginal rock art can be found at sites throughout Australia. Some examples are believed to depict more recent historical events, such as the arrival of European ships.
Many of Sydney Parkinson's drawings were met with scepticism when taken back to Europe. For example, claims that the platypus was a hoax.

Macassan fishermen came to Arnhem Land to harvest trepang, and the earliest recorded voyage was in 1751. Anthropologists note that Arnhem Land rock art, along with other evidence, suggests contact around 1640.

Bark painting, done with ochres on dried bark stripped from trees, is an old Aboriginal tradition. The earliest European find was in a shelter in Tasmania around 1800, and other painted bark shelters were found in Victoria and New South Wales.

war.text: The first conflict between Indigenous Australians and British settlers took place only several months after the First Fleet landed in January 1788. In May 1788, five convicts were killed and an Indigenous man was wounded. Relations had turned tense as the British cleared land and caught fish.

The first frontier war began in 1795, when British settlers established farms along the Hawkesbury River west of Sydney. Some of these farms were set up by soldiers to provide security to the region. Local Darug people raided the farms until Governor Macquarie sent a detachment of the 46th Regiment of Foot in 1816, which ended the conflict by killing 14 Indigenous Australians in an ambush on their campsite.

In 1772, a French expedition under Marion Dufresne visited Tasmania, and contact with the Aboriginal people was at first friendly. The Aboriginal Tasmanians became alarmed when another boat was sent toward the shore, and spears and stones were reportedly thrown. The French responded with musket fire, killing at least one Aboriginal person and wounding several others.

Governor Arthur Phillip was instructed to live in amity and kindness with Indigenous Australians, and he tried to avoid conflict. After being speared in 1790, he forbade reprisals. Language barriers made communication extremely difficult.

In December 1790, Phillip authorised two punitive expeditions after his huntsman was killed by an Indigenous warrior named Pemulwuy. Neither expedition was successful. It was a notable step for a governor who had earlier tried to avoid conflict.

In June 1788, the British grew increasingly concerned when groups of up to three hundred Indigenous people were sighted at the outskirts of the colony. Despite this, Governor Phillip kept trying to avoid conflict.

Pemulwuy led Indigenous Australians in raids around Parramatta between 1795 and 1802. These attacks led Governor Philip Gidley King to issue an order in 1801 authorising settlers to shoot Indigenous Australians on sight in the Parramatta, Georges River and Prospect areas.

literature.text: For centuries before British settlement, European writers wrote fictional accounts of an imagined Great Southern Land. The land was a literary idea long before it was a colony. Australian writing has explored the continent's character since 1788.

Watkin Tench, a British officer, arrived with the First Fleet in 1788 and later published two books about the foundations of New South Wales. Robert Hughes and Thomas Keneally consider his humane accounts essential reading on early Australian history.
A letter written by Bennelong to Governor Arthur Phillip in 1796 is the first known work written in English by an Aboriginal person. It opens the story of Indigenous Australian literature.

In 1642 Abel Janszoon Tasman landed in Tasmania and examined notches cut at considerable distances on tree trunks. He speculated that the newly discovered country must be peopled by giants. It is an early European guess about the land, written before any settlement.

In 1797 the British Romantic poet Robert Southey, then a young Jacobin, published a collection called Poems. It included a section titled "Botany Bay Eclogues", which portrayed the plight and stories of convicts transported to New South Wales.

Aboriginal myths across Australia together form a kind of unwritten, oral library, in which Aboriginal peoples learn about the world. Many versions of a "Captain Cook" story exist, in which he arrives from the sea bringing British rule, and he is more often a villain than a hero. In a version told by Rolly Gilbert, people are shot down like animals and left lying for the hawks and crows, and in a Victoria River version the Aboriginal peoples of the Sydney area are massacred. These versions are rarely recollections of the real James Cook, though the Guugu Yimidhirr did meet him in 1770 while the Endeavour was beached for seven weeks for repairs.
The British satirist Jonathan Swift set the land of the Houyhnhnms from Gulliver's Travels to the west of Tasmania. The southern lands, barely known to Europeans, became a place for imagined worlds.

Tench's two books were Narrative of the Expedition to Botany Bay and Complete Account of the Settlement at Port Jackson. Written with a spirit of humanity, they are considered by writers including Robert Hughes and Thomas Keneally to be essential reading for early Australian history.

literature.text: Nearly all Indigenous Australian literature is in English, because Indigenous Australians had not written their languages before colonisation. Bennelong's 1796 letter to Governor Arthur Phillip was written in English too.
Wiradjuri writer and academic Anita Heiss has edited a collection of Aboriginal literature that spans from 1796 until 2008. Its starting year matches Bennelong's letter to Governor Arthur Phillip.

science.text: HMS Endeavour was purchased by the Royal Navy for a scientific mission to the Pacific, reaching Tahiti in time to observe the 1769 transit of Venus. In September 1769 she anchored off New Zealand, becoming the first European ship to reach the islands since Abel Tasman's Heemskerck, 127 years earlier.
In April 1770, HMS Endeavour became the first European ship to reach the east coast of Australia. Captain James Cook went ashore at what is now known as Botany Bay.

Naturalist Joseph Banks sailed with Captain James Cook on HMS Endeavour from 1768 to 1771, visiting Brazil, Tahiti, New Zealand and Australia. He brought home 30,000 plant specimens, becoming the first European to document 1,400 of them.

Aboriginal Australians developed astronomical knowledge passed down through oral tradition, naming constellations such as the Pleiades, Orion and the Emu in the Sky. They used this knowledge to build calendars and navigate across the continent.

After his voyage with Cook, Joseph Banks became the greatest proponent of British settlement in New South Wales and of the colonisation of Australia. He also advocated Botany Bay as a place for the reception of convicts, and advised the British government on all Australian matters for twenty years. Ships from New South Wales brought him plants, animals, specimens and, on at least one occasion, human remains: Governor Philip Gidley King sent Banks the severed head of an Aboriginal man named Pemulwuy, whom Banks had seemingly listed among his "desiderata".

On 11 June 1770, HMS Endeavour struck a reef within the Great Barrier Reef system just before 11:00 pm and went hard aground. Captain James Cook ordered all but four of the ship's guns thrown overboard, along with ballast and spoiled stores, and the drinking water pumped out. Every man on board, Cook and Banks included, took turns on the pumps as a hole in the hull let water in. The ship was 24 miles from shore and her three boats could not carry the whole crew, so sinking would have been grim; she floated off on the next evening's tide, and was then beached on the Australian mainland for seven weeks for repairs.

When James Cook set off in 1768 to circumnavigate the world aboard HM Bark Endeavour, malt and wort were the top scurvy remedies he was ordered to investigate. The theory behind them was backed by Surgeon General Sir John Pringle.

After James Cook's 1769 visit and Marion du Fresne's longer stay in 1772, Māori in New Zealand obtained iron and steel for the first time. They quickly adopted the new material, especially for woodcarving.

For the Pitjantjatjara, the rising of the Pleiades at dawn each May marked the start of winter. The Boorong people of Victoria knew that when the Malleefowl constellation disappeared in October, it was time to gather her eggs.

Cook's anti-scurvy provisions also included beer and sauerkraut, but the list notably excluded lemons. This was despite naval surgeon James Lind having demonstrated in 1747 that citrus fruit could treat scurvy.
Māori woodcarvers learned to ask European sailors to sharpen eight-inch-long ship's nails into chisel points on a ship's wheel. They traded fish in exchange for these sharpened iron tools.

politics.text: British colonisation of Australia began in 1788 with the establishment of the penal colony of New South Wales. Before that, Australia's written history had started with Dutch exploration of most of the coastline in the 17th century.
In 1770, English navigator James Cook claimed the east coast of Australia for the British Empire. He did so without conducting negotiations with the existing inhabitants.

In 1606 the crew of the Dutch ship Duyfken, captained by Willem Janszoon, made the first documented European landing in Australia. It was also the first contact with Aboriginal Australians. Later that year, Luís Vaz de Torres sailed to the north of Australia through Torres Strait.
In 1770 and again in 1788, the British Empire claimed Eastern Australia as its own. It based the claim on the doctrine of terra nullius, which is now discredited.

Abel Tasman's voyage of 1642 was the first known European expedition to reach Van Diemen's Land. On his second voyage of 1644 he mapped the north coast of Australia. After his voyages the Dutch named the continent New Holland.

The first Governor of New South Wales, Arthur Phillip, was expressly instructed to establish friendship and good relations with Aboriginal people. Even so, interactions between early settlers and Indigenous people varied considerably throughout the colonial period.
Bennelong and a companion became the first Australians to sail to Europe. There they met King George III. Bennelong had been an early go-between with the settlers at Sydney, showing mutual curiosity.
Pemulwuy of the Sydney region showed outright hostility to the settlers. He was accused of the first killing of a white settler in 1790.

philosophy.text: In Aboriginal belief, the Dreaming describes a time of "Everywhen", when ancestral figures, often of heroic proportions or with supernatural abilities, inhabited and created the land. The meaning of specific places and creatures is tied to their origin in the Dreaming. This gave the whole landscape a spiritual meaning.

Australian Indigenous traditions place moral authority outside the individual, in the Dreaming. This authority is bound up with the relation of human society to the land. Right conduct was therefore tied to country rather than to personal opinion.

Christianity came to Australia in 1788 with British colonial settlement. Most convicts and free settlers belonged to the established Church of England, with smaller numbers of Nonconformist Protestants, Catholics and others. This introduced a new religious tradition to a continent that had followed the Dreaming.

Long before British settlement in 1788, Muslim fishermen from Makassar visited north-western Australia. Their graves for comrades who died on the journey face Mecca, following Islamic burial rules. Aboriginal cave paintings and ceremonies also show Makassan canoe designs and words.

The Murrinh-Patha people describe a Dreamtime that anthropologists see as giving them a oneness of thought, belief, and expression unequalled within Christianity. They draw no line between the spiritual and the material, or between the sacred and the profane. All life is sacred, and all conduct carries moral weight.

In Aboriginal thought the Dreaming can also serve as a system of totemic symbols. A person may own a specific Dreaming, such as a kangaroo Dreaming or a Honey Ant Dreaming. Because an individual's whole ancestry exists as one continuing cycle, all worldly knowledge is understood to be accumulated through one's ancestors.

Mircea Eliade wrote that Indigenous Australians generally believe the world, humans, animals and plants were created by Supernatural beings. These beings afterwards disappeared, either ascending to the sky or entering the earth. Aboriginal spirituality remains intrinsically linked to the land and to certain sites of significance.

Aboriginal stories are said to layer the whole Australian continent's topography with cultural nuance and deeper meaning. They pass the accumulated wisdom and knowledge of ancestors to selected audiences. Some Aboriginal myths also describe ancient landscapes, such as the volcanic origins of lakes dated to more than 10,000 years ago.

Torres Strait Islander religion bore similarities to broader Melanesian spirituality, and is a separate Indigenous tradition from the Aboriginal Dreaming. Together these traditions formed the religious landscape of the region before the British arrived in 1788.

culture.text: Aboriginal Australians had one of the oldest living cultures in the world. By the time of British settlement, they spoke more than 250 distinct languages.

Before the British arrived, Aboriginal Australians were nomadic and often travelled over extensive distances. They relied on hunting, gathering and fishing, and their intricate social structure was deeply connected to the land and to beliefs about the spiritual realm. After 1788 these ways of life began to change or disappear as Aboriginal Australians were forced to compete with settlers. Conflict, fuelled by misunderstanding and prejudice, saw indigenous people subjugated, with some killed and others forcibly removed from their traditional territories, and European-borne diseases sharply raised mortality rates.

Aboriginal spirituality includes the Dreaming, songlines and oral literature. Rituals allow a person to return to Dreamtime, reconnecting the spirit with nature, with ancestors and with their own place in the scheme of things.

Macassan fishermen made annual expeditions to Arnhem Land and the Kimberley to harvest trepang, or sea cucumber, to sell to the Chinese. Anthropologists note the significant impact of this industry on the Yolngu people, with signs of contact around 1640.

At the height of the trepang industry, an estimated 1,000 Macassan arrived each December with the start of the monsoon season. They set up semi-permanent camps to prepare the trepang and trade with the Yolngu people, then sailed home four months later to sell their cargo.

The Guugu Yimidhirr people encountered James Cook during a seven-week period when the Endeavour was beached for repairs on the Endeavour River. The Guugu Yimidhirr still recollect this encounter, and from that time they received present-day names for places in their local landscape.

In 1770, James Cook feared the French had beaten him to the claim. He turned a hilltop signal-drill on Possession Island in Torres Strait into a possession ceremony, fabricating Britain's claim to Australia's east coast. Eighteen years later Britain occupied the east coast, at a time when the indigenous population was estimated at between 315,000 and 750,000.
The Yolngu word Balanda, used for European people, comes originally from the Makassarese language. It travelled via the Malay phrase orang belanda, meaning Dutch person.
In 1773, Captain Tobias Furneaux visited Tasmania on the Resolution and made no contact with Aboriginal Tasmanians. He did leave gifts for them in unoccupied shelters found on Bruny Island.

In 1772, a French expedition under Marion Dufresne visited Tasmania, and contact with Aboriginal people was at first friendly. The Aboriginal Tasmanians became alarmed when another boat was sent towards the shore, and spears and stones were reportedly thrown. The French responded with musket fire, killing at least one Aboriginal person and wounding several others.

In 1770 James Cook's Endeavour was beached for seven weeks for repairs at the site of present-day Cooktown. The Guugu Yimidhirr people along the Endeavour River met Cook during this time. They still recall the encounter, and received present-day names for places in their local landscape from it.

Bennelong and a companion became the first Australians to sail to Europe, where they met King George III. Bungaree accompanied the explorer Matthew Flinders on the first circumnavigation of Australia.
